downstream_reviews.source_excerpt:
1. Call [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]] in its complex branch.
   Propagate any non-Schur status. Treat its returned $Q,T$ as candidates.
2. Verify by exact arithmetic that $Q^*Q=I$, $A=QTQ^*$, and $T$ is upper
   triangular. If any identity fails, return schur-certificate-failure. The
   computed Schur routine's residual diagnostic alone does not pass this test.
3. Start from the supplied contiguous block partition of $T$. For each block
   $T_{ii}$ call [[alg-exact-jordan-block-analytic-evaluation]] with its exact
   Jordan certificate and return value $F_{ii}$. If a certificate or required
   derivative is missing, return missing-jordan-data.
4. Visit block pairs by increasing distance $j-i$. Form
   $$C_{ij}=F_{ii}T_{ij}-T_{ij}F_{jj} +\sum_{i<k<j}(F_{ik}T_{kj}-T_{ik}F_{kj}).$$
   Call [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]] on
   $T_{ii}F_{ij}+F_{ij}(-T_{jj})=C_{ij}$ with threshold $\tau$. If it returns
   `success`, store its exact solution as $F_{ij}$. If it returns `singular-pivot` or
   `pivot-separation-failure` and the partition has multiple blocks, merge the
   contiguous blocks from $i$ through $j$, discard their old diagonal data,
   and restart step 3. Each merge reduces the block count, so there are at most
   $n-1$ merges. Any other non-success status is returned as
   inconclusive-sylvester with its underlying status.
5. Return the factored value $QFQ^*$ with status parlett-success.

downstream_reviews.source_excerpt: 1.1 Hessenberg reduction uses at most $\max(n-2,0)$ reflector steps. For $n\ge3$, forming one reflector costs $O(n)$ scalar operations, and applying its two-sided similarity to the remaining dense submatrix costs $O(n^2)$; summing over at most $n$ steps gives $O(n^3)$. Any full initialization zero-pattern checks also cost at most $O(n^2)$ per stage, hence at most $O(n^3)$ in total. For $n=1,2$, there are no such reflector stages and no below-subdiagonal entries. [F2, algebra]

downstream_reviews.source_excerpt: 3.1 After initialization's full pattern check, every position below the first subdiagonal is zero; for $n\le2$ there is no such position. A block chase on $[a,b]$ changes matrix entries only in rows or columns of that interval: every left update and target overwrite has a row in it, and every right update has a column in it. Its complementary below-subdiagonal entries therefore stay unchanged and zero. The explicit row ranges in [F1] test every remaining below-subdiagonal position, without repetition and in row-major order. An accepted block check thus establishes the entire global Hessenberg pattern again; a rejected check detects exactly a nonzero entry that a full row-major pattern check would first detect at the same block boundary. Deflation writes are on the first subdiagonal, so preserve this invariant. Induction over all processed blocks and scans proves that the final target check starts from a globally verified Hessenberg matrix. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]
